A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same answer-attribution study and FARL framework. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across additions, relocation, and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original perturbation experiments, attention-head probing, and FARL training evaluations, including Tables 1–2 and the additional results in Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds activation-patching experiments, logit trajectories, memory-editing validation, free-form QA evaluation, and cue-position tests.

M1.justification: FARL's training procedure and GRPO/NPO objectives are unchanged. Appendix D.2 makes a limited adaptation to the diagnostic perturbation procedure: GPT-5-mini generates misleading free-form answers, whereas the original multiple-choice procedure selects retrieval targets using incorrect-answer logits.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates multiple-choice QA on MMLU, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, and GPQA. v2 extends evaluation to 400 GeneralThought free-form questions requiring numerical, noun, or short-phrase answers, substantially broadening the answer-generation requirements. Appendix D.1 also evaluates paraphrased questions within the retained domains.

E2.justification: The new activation-patching experiment compares AUC-selected attention heads against randomly selected heads. FARL's base-model, SFT, and GRPO comparators remain unchanged in Tables 1–2. ROME and MEMIT are discussed in Appendix D.1 but are not newly evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds bidirectional activation patching of the top 5% of heads, stepwise answer-logit probing, 400-question free-form evaluation, paraphrase testing on 50 selected examples per domain, locality checks with and without CoT, and beginning-versus-end cue insertion. These substantially extend the evaluation design. Original training budgets and settings are retained; the newly stated training/validation counts are disclosures rather than established split changes.

E4.justification: Section 3.4 adds causal tests of attention-head involvement and four reasoning-step logit case studies. Appendix D adds analyses of editing efficacy, paraphrase robustness, unrelated-domain locality, and sensitivity to cue position. These test important attribution assumptions beyond v1's correlational probes and existing supplementary analyses.

E5.justification: No repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, or significance tests are added or revised. Existing five-fold probing and reasoning-trajectory distribution displays are retained; the new experiments report point estimates without additional uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 and all original plotted results are retained. Newly reported activation-patching success rates are 87.2% versus 5.3% for restoring answers and 89.5% versus 2.1% for inducing perturbed answers, comparing selected with random heads. Figure 6 and Tables 3–7 add logit trajectories, editing-validation results, free-form QA scores, and cue-position outcomes. These are additional results, not improved scores under the original FARL settings.

T1.justification: Appendix D.1 introduces mathematical success conditions for the newly evaluated editing efficacy, paraphrase generalization, and locality metrics. Existing perturbation/PER definitions and FARL equations (1)–(4) remain unchanged. There are no new theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the dual reasoning/retrieval account, the same dominance factors, and FARL's claimed contribution. The headline improvements of 47.8%, 22.8%, and 5.8% are unchanged. Added experiments support the existing core claims.

C2.justification: v2 interprets activation patching as causal evidence of head-level control and logit trajectories as competition throughout reasoning. Appendix D adds arguments about editing locality, applicability beyond multiple-choice QA, and limited positional confounding. Section 4.1 also qualifies retrieval interference as a potential risk. The original limitations concerning longer traces and untested larger models remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link and a reproducibility statement describing training/evaluation code, preprocessing scripts, and dataset-version information. It discloses 1,353 training and 147 validation samples, grid-search use, and procedural details for the new analyses, including head selection, step segmentation, and GPT-5-mini usage. Repository contents are not verified by the supplied PDFs.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds focused comparisons with concurrent memorization-attribution and latent-CoT studies, plus newer faithfulness and RL citations. Appendix D.1 positions SFT editing against fact-editing methods such as ROME and MEMIT, while Appendix B.2 adds grid-search citations. These expand the context without replacing the paper's central research positioning.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are preserved. v2 adds analysis subsections, Appendix D, an appendix contents list, ethics/reproducibility statements, and acknowledgements; it also refines appendix headings, makes local language edits, and updates affiliations and publication headers. There is no extensive rewriting of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds a four-panel logit-trajectory figure and five tables displaying editing validity, free-form QA, and cue-position results, substantially extending the visual evidence. All ten original figures and Tables 1–2 are retained, with relocation and figure renumbering rather than substantive redraws.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central mechanistic argument by supplementing v1's correlational head probes with bidirectional activation patching and random-head controls. Free-form evaluation and locality/position checks address previously untested assumptions, while code-access and split disclosures improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh reporting concerns in the new appendix: Tables 3–4 contain identical values, and rates such as 0.975 are unexplained for the stated 50 paraphrase examples per domain. Those issues limit confidence in part of the added evidence.
